summary: Describes a mechanism for mixing additional master secret inputs into TLS and DTLS key derivation. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6358 lets certain TLS and DTLS extensions contribute extra data when the connection's master secret is calculated. The data from multiple extensions is included in a defined order so both sides calculate the same secret.

subtitle: A framework for TLS extensions to add input to master-secret calculation.

tldr.problem: Some TLS and DTLS extensions need their data included in the calculation of the master secret.
tldr.mechanism: An extension can specify additional input, which is combined with the client and server random values in the PRF calculation; multiple inputs are ordered by extension type.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6358 describes an Experimental framework for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 extensions.

today: RFC 6358 is Experimental. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Add Master Secret Input
sections.content: Some TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 extensions want particular data mixed into the calculation of the master secret. The RFC describes this as binding the added material directly into the secret used to protect the session. It provides a framework for extensions to identify themselves as extensions with master secret input.
sections.plainLanguage: An extension may need its data to affect the connection's master secret. This framework gives it a defined way to include that data.

sections.title: How Additional Input Is Combined
sections.content: When the handshake includes an extension with master secret input, its additional values MUST be mixed into the pseudorandom function calculation with the client and server random values. Inputs from multiple extensions MUST be ordered by extension type. The RFC requires this order so the client and server can calculate the same master secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides add the extra values in the same agreed order when calculating the secret. This lets them reach the same result.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that additional input may be predictable and may increase the amount of data an attacker can inject into the calculation. It states that the TLS pseudorandom function is designed to work with predictable material and that predictable additional input does not harm the resulting output. When the additional values contain entropy, that entropy is reflected in the output.
sections.plainLanguage: Additional input does not need to be secret or unpredictable for the calculation to work as described. Any entropy in it is reflected in the output.
